title: Short Stuff: Time Zones
summary: Short Stuff episode on time zones. The hosts describe how local solar time made travel and train scheduling difficult, and how the US went from hundreds of local times to four standard zones after railroad companies agreed on uniform time on November 18, 1883, the "day of two Noons." They cover Sandford Fleming's proposal of 24 zones after a missed train in 1876, the modern count of about 39 zones with some offset by 30 or 45 minutes, and the proposal by physicist Hanka (Johns Hopkins) and Richard Henry to adopt Coordinated Universal Time (UTC, formerly Greenwich Mean Time, also called Zulu time) worldwide. They discuss the generational adjustment this would take, whether it would help jet lag, and the likelihood the US would not adopt it.

segments.title: Opening banter and why time zones are new
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short episode on time zones and note that time zones became important only once faster travel made nearby towns' times matter.

segments.title: Railroads and missed trains
segments.summary: Discussion of how faster trains made scheduling across towns difficult, causing missed connections and near collisions, especially in Europe and the US.

segments.title: Local time in the US and the number of time zones
segments.summary: Before standardization, each US town kept its own noon based on the sun, producing hundreds of local times; the count was reduced to about one hundred before standard zones.

segments.title: Sandford Fleming and the 24 time zones
segments.summary: Sandford Fleming, a Scottish scientist, reportedly proposed dividing the world into zones after missing a train in 1876. The hosts note the world now has about 39 zones, some offset by 30 or 45 minutes.

segments.title: Railroads adopt four US time zones and the day of two Noons
segments.summary: Railroad companies adopted uniform standard time for Eastern, Central, Mountain and Pacific zones on November 18, 1883, so some places had noon twice in one day.

segments.title: Breaking and wheeldy
segments.summary: A brief light exchange about the word unwieldy and the hosts moving on to planes and the internet.

segments.title: Proposal for universal time (UTC)
segments.summary: Hanka and Richard Henry propose that everyone set clocks to UTC, formerly Greenwich Mean Time and called Zulu time. The hosts discuss how this would change meaning of clock times and how long adoption would take, possibly a generation. They discuss jet lag and business benefits, and doubt the US would adopt it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and mention the show's production credit.
